en: Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, Vāsudeva, the eternal, as well as Gaṇādhipa and the Goddess of Speech, I shall expound the science of phonetics (Śikṣā) according to my understanding.

Now the traditional enumeration of phonemes (varṇasamāmnāya) is stated: here, according to the Yajurvedic tradition, the first nine phonemes are short vowels; among these, the two pairs consisting of the short and long vowels are considered homogeneous (savarṇa), but not including those preceded by a protracted (pluta) vowel.

There are sixteen vowels at the beginning of that [alphabet]; the remainder are known as consonants (vyañjana). Among the consonants, the first twenty-five are declared to be the "contacts" (sparśa); the next four are the "semivowels" (antasthā), and after those follow the six "sibilants" (ūṣman). 3–4.
The groups of consonants (varga) consist of five each, following the sequence of the *sparśas*;
their designations are, in order, the first and so forth, while the fifth group is called the "excellent" (*uttama*).
Visarga and the second letters of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), as are the first letters; however, *ha* is not [unvoiced].

Ghoṣavat, vyañjanaśeṣa, paryāṇi, adhi, abhi, viprati, pra, ava, upa, and eti are prefixes (upasarga). A phoneme followed by the letter 'ka' is called a *varṇa*; that same [term] applies to consonants when they are separated by the letter 'a'. (6–7)

In this [system], there are the *visarjanīya*, *anusvāra*, and *upadhmānīya*, as well as the *jihvāmūlīya* and *nāsikya*; among these, the *repha* (the sound *r*) belongs to the *ras* (the retroflex class).
For the three [consonants] following a vowel, the short *akāra* (*a*) may serve as the *hal* (consonant) suffix.
The short vowels *ṛ* and *ḷ*, the anusvāra, as well as *a*, *i*, and *u*, [are termed *hrasva*].
Furthermore, the letter following each class [of consonants] is called by the name of that class; likewise, the first [letter of each class] is also [so named].
This is the *paribhāṣā*.

Now I shall describe the characteristics of the four types, beginning with the sequence of pure syllables (*śuddhavarṇakrama*), which constitute the essence of the sequence of syllables (*varṇasāra*). First, the method for the *varṇasāra* is correctly explained.

The sound, the place of articulation, the organ, the effort, the deity, the genus, the limb, and the designation by class— these are prescribed for the consonants in this manner, beginning with the sound and so forth, according to their sequence.
(12) This is declared for the vowels as well, starting from the sound and so on, in due order.
The duration of a *mātrā* is proclaimed as being between the time required for effort (*prayatna*) and that of a deity (*deva*).

One should not mention the limbs (*aṅga*) of vowels or consonants taken individually; however, regarding the accents such as the acute (*udātta*), one should avoid [mentioning] the sounds (*dhvani*) and so forth. 13–14.

Nevertheless, the lineage, class, and qualities of the deities; the observation of lines and so forth; the state of the limbs and other parts; the cause of the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*; their points of origin; and their respective names, [should be known] in their proper sequence.

One should also apply here those dharmas taught in the scriptures regarding the pure vowels; having joined them accordingly in their respective places, one should state the qualities such as *bhakti* and so forth.
The dharma of the consonant is eightfold, and likewise that of the vowel is eightfold.
The ten properties of vowels such as low (*nīca*), high (*ucca*), and so forth, have been proclaimed; furthermore,
for a single vowel conjoined with consonants such as *ucca* and others,
twenty-six properties are stated— this is what has been illustrated here.
The wise know this sequence of phonemes to be the essence of all colors (or qualities).
Thus ends the second chapter.
Now follows the origin of sound from the impelling of the body-wind.
Its origin is proclaimed to be at the junction of the throat and the chest.
Here, its five resonances (prātiśrutkāni) are as follows: the chest, the throat, the head, the mouth, and the two cavities of the nose. 20–21.

When the throat is constricted, there is breath; when it is open, the sound *ha* is produced. Between these two are the primary elements of the phonemes (varṇaprakṛti). Furthermore, in the case of voiced consonants (*aghoṣavat*), *nāda* serves as the secondary articulation (*anupradāna*).

The sound *ha* occurs in the fourth [class of consonants] and indeed in the unvoiced [aspirates]; it is accompanied by breath. These very sounds are known to be most prominent in the first [class of consonants].
When there is no vowel, the jaws and lips should not be excessively separated, nor should they be excessively closed.
When producing the vowel *u*, the tongue should be brought close to the palate;

when producing the vowel *ū*, there is a specific requirement here: the lips must be drawn closer together than in the case of the preceding vowel. This [contraction] should be performed at the midpoint of the inherent [vowel], not half of it.

In the case of the labials, first one brings the tip of the tongue close [to the teeth]; in the case of the *trika* (the three consonants *ta*, *tha*, *da*), the two jaws should be more closely drawn together, and the two lips should be slightly protruded like the letter *a*; when the jaws are very closely drawn together, the lips remain as before. 26–27.
For the *jambhya* sounds, one touches them with the upper part of the tongue between the inner edges of the jaws; for *e*, as before, on the palate; for *i*, like the middle of the tongue; 28.
for *o*, the jaws are not too wide apart and the lips are fully drawn together.
The organ of articulation for *ai* and *au* is the same as that for *e* and *o* respectively.
According to some, the initial portion of *ai* and *au* is said to be half an *a*-sound; for them, that [initial portion] possesses a more contracted (*saṃvṛtatara*) organ of articulation. (29–30)

The *ikāra* (the vowel *i*) is one-and-a-half [mātrās] long; it should be the remainder of the preceding [syllable], while for the following [syllable], the properties of being nasalized (*anunāsika*) should apply, as should the *anusvāra*, even at the end. Where there is a convergence (*upasaṃhāra*) of vowels, that place [of articulation] is employed here.
One should know that the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) of vowels is that which brings them together;
however, when there is contact with the point of articulation (*sthāna*), that is to be known as the "instrument" of consonants, by means of which one touches [the place of articulation]. (32–33)
One touches the root of the jaw with the *ka*-group, and likewise the root of the tongue;
then one touches the palate with the *ca*-group using the middle of the tongue;
and having encircled [the palate], one touches the head with the *ṭa*-group using the tip of the tongue.
One touches the *tavarga* with the tip of the tongue at the lower part of the roots of the teeth; then the *pavarga* with the lower lip against the upper lip;
and likewise, the letter *ya* with both the middle and the end of the tongue against the palate.
The letter *ra* is produced by the middle of the tip of the tongue against the roots of the upper teeth;
*la* is produced by the two ends of the lips; and *va* is produced by the tips of the upper teeth.
(37) The five sibilants (*ūṣman*) are produced in their respective order at the places of articulation of the stops (*sparśa*).
Among those [articulatory efforts], the middle effort (karaṇa) is open (vivṛta) here;
the throat (kaṇṭha) is the place (sthāna), and that same [effort] is the articulatory effort for both the emission of breath (havisarga) and [the other sounds].
However, there is chest-resonance (urasyatva) in the case of the letter *ha* when it is followed by an *uttama* (nasal) or a semivowel (*antastha*). 38–39.

The *nāsikya*s are those whose place of articulation is the nose, or they may be articulated by both mouth and nose; here, as in the case of the consonant groups (*varga*), there is a combination of places of articulation. Regarding these, [the rule] "but among them... (40) applies. Thus ends the third chapter.
The effort (*prayatna*) for vowels and sibilants (*ūṣman*) is *vivṛta* (open), while for the letter *a* alone it is *saṃhṛta* (contracted).

Indeed, the letters from *k* to *m* are produced by *spṛṣṭa* (contact); then, for the first four [classes], there is a slight [contact] at the beginning. The second and fourth letters of each class are produced by *ati-spṛṣṭa* (excessive contact). Thus, the effort is fivefold.

Wind, fire, earth, moon, and sun shall be the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the vowels and consonant groups. The letters *a*, the group beginning with *ka* (*kavarga*), the first letter (*a*), and the wind (*vāyu*) are designated as Indra; *i*, *e*, the second letter (*i*), and those known as Indra and fire (*vahni*) are Bhauma; *u*, the group beginning with *ca* (*cavarga*), the third letter (*u*), and the moon (*candra*) are Āditya; and *ṛ*, the group beginning with *ṭa* (*ṭavarga*), the fourth letter (*ṛ*), and *va*, *i*, *au* are Candra. (42–43)

The fifty phonemes have been well-sung by the sages as follows: those ending with the letter *ḷ* belong to the Sun; the first letters of each consonant-group (*ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*) belong to Brahmā; the vowels belong to the Kṣatriyas; likewise, the second, third, and fourth letters of each group belong to the Kṣatriyas;

the four letters beginning with *ya* belong to the Vaiśyas; and the final letters (*na*, *ma*, *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*), along with the *anusvāra*, *visarga*, and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), belong to the Śūdras. 44.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.

That consonant which [occurs] is a limb of the preceding vowel; however, that which has become its limb is a limb of the subsequent vowel. But a nasal (*naḥ*) occurring at the end of a word (*avasānavartin*) when joined with a following vowel (*parāyukta*) is not [a limb of the preceding vowel], provided it is not *saṃnyuta*. 45.

The *anusvāra* and *visarga* belonging to the *yoga* (conjunction) [of consonants], as well as the *bhakti* (fractional sound), likewise become *repha* (r-sound) when followed by the vowel *ṛ*. (46) If a *sparśa* (stop consonant) follows a *ūṣman* (sibilant), it does not belong to the preceding vowel; nevertheless, the *vikṛti* (modification) remains a *bhakti* belonging to the subsequent member. Furthermore, when held [as such] and followed by *ṛ*, the *repha* likewise belongs to the subsequent member due to its accumulation (*pracaya*). (47)

Where a non-homogeneous consonant follows a following vowel (*parasvara*), it is an *aṅga* (subordinate) only if it arises after a semi-vowel (*antastha*); for when a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows, the contact consonant (*sparśa*) and the *yamas* are indeed subordinate to the following vowel.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.

Vowels (*ac*) are [the sounds] *a* through *au*. Consonants (*vyañjana*) are the stops (*sparśa*), the sibilants and *h* (*hal*), the unvoiced (*avaghoṣa*), the semivowels (*antastha*), the aspirates (*ūṣman*), and the voiced (*ghoṣa*). The last letters of each class (*uttama*), as well as the first letters of each class (*ādya*), and likewise the short (*hrasva*), long (*dīrgha*), and protracted (*pluta*) vowels, and so forth—these are the technical designations for phonemes (*varṇasaṃjñā*). 49. Thus ends the sixth chapter.
In the forest, the *kikīdivī* bird naturally cries for the duration of one *mātrā*, which is short (*hrasva*);
the crow cries for twice that time, which constitutes two *mātrās* and is long (*dīrgha*);
the peacock speaks for three *mātrās*, which is protracted (*pluta*); and the mongoose cries for half the time of a short vowel, which is a half-*mātrā*.

The ground belongs to the *ucca*, fire to the *nihata*, the moon to the *svāra*, and the sun to the *pracaya*. The *virāj* is the low-born Brahmin caste, the *svāra* is the Vaiśya, and the *pracaya* is the Śūdra.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.
The *svāra* and *udātta* accents belong to the *rājasa* and *sāttvika* qualities, while the *dhṛta* and *anudātta* accents belong to the *tāmasa* quality.
(52) Thus ends the eighth chapter.
One should indicate the *udātta* on the middle joint of the index finger (*tarjanī*), and the *nīca* (anudātta) on the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*) and so forth.

One should indicate the *svarita* accent on the final syllable of the ring finger (*anāmikā*), and the *pracaya* accent on the middle finger (*madhyamā*). That which is called the "accent" (*svara*) arising from the division [of the fingers] is distinct; the positions of the fingers for the acute (*udātta*) and other accents are as follows:
if the tone is high, like something raised upward, it belongs to the middle and the end of the ring finger. (53–54)
When there is a vibration of one's own [vocal organs], the *svarita* and *anudātta* accents are indicated respectively by the last and first lines of the ring finger;
when there is a high vibration, the *udātta* and *nīca* (low) accents are indicated by the index and middle fingers.
That [vowel] would not exist at the time of the pause of the consonant alone; it attains its separate position prior [to the consonant].
The wise one should demonstrate the shape of a cow's ear with the tip of the thumb on the right hand (56).
Having sequentially fixed the mind, the gaze, and the hand upon the vowels, he should apply himself to this;
for he who studies this Veda with his hand, while reflecting upon the phonemes, accents, and meanings (57).
Purified by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman verses, he is eternally honored in that world of Brahman.

The length of the vocal organs, the firmness of the sound, as well as the narrowness of the cavity of the throat—these produce the loudness of the sound; whereas the shortness [of the organs] is the softness of the tone. (58)
These [vocal organs], which are expanded within the cavity of the throat, constantly produce the struck sound.
(59) Thus ends the ninth chapter.
Gāndhāra and Madhyama are born from the high [register], while Ṣaḍja and Ṛṣabha are both produced from the struck [register].

That fifth [note], Dhaivata, and Niṣāda, along with three other notes, are born from the *svarita* accent (60). Among those, the constant (*nitya*) and the struck (*nihata*)—these two, together with the momentary (*kṣaipra*) Niṣāda, would be the causes for the fifth note; likewise, those two, known as *praśliṣṭaka* and *prātihata*, would serve as the causes for the fifth note (61).

Likewise, in the commentary on the final *svaraka* foot, there should be [the notes] that serve as the causes for *dhaivata*; furthermore, for *gāndhāra* and also for *madhyama*, there should be *udātta* and *pracaya* respectively, in sequence.
(62) Now, if the long and short [syllables] are *anudātta*, they are the causes for *ṣaḍja* and *ṛṣabha* respectively. (63)
Touching simultaneously the chest, the throat, the teeth, the palate, the tongue,
and the nose— from these six, because this sound is born, it is therefore called *ṣaḍja* here in this world. (64) Arising from the navel as a light wind, it is struck by the throat and the head.

Because it bellows like a bull (*ṛṣabha*) with a low sound, it is therefore known as *ṛṣabha*. Because it is a cow (*gauḥ*) that possesses height (*ucca*) and sustains [the sound], or because it cries out "tām vai gandhā" and "ajā se," it is the *gāndhāra*, characterized by the quality of being produced through effort arising in the upper part [of the vocal tract]. 65–66.

Because its own notes (*svaras*) are situated in the middle, it is called *madhyama*; furthermore, the wind arising from the navel, as it moves through the five locations—the chest region, the heart, the throat, the head, and the root of the ear—and emerges from the throat, it becomes the *pañcama* (fifth) note. Thus it should be understood.
Because he is the "middle" (*madhyama*) among all seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*, or because he is sung by cuckoos (*pika*) at that time;

and because this *dhaivata* is specifically intended and sounded as the final note (*svarānta*), it subsequently establishes itself at the edge of the forehead due to the power of its predominance in the *tāna* scale. 68–69.

Because they sit (*niṣīdanti*) upon this, it is called *niṣāda*; therefore, it subsequently pervades and remains throughout the entire junctional region (*sandhipradeśa*), having a form similar to the sound of an elephant.
First, the sound that has arisen is heard as a short measure; the learned call this *śruti*, which is the primary constituent part of the musical note (*svara*).

Those well-versed in the various *Bhārata* traditions state that the designations for its notes (*svara*) as *sa*, *ri*, *ga*, *ma*, *pa*, *dha*, and *ni* were indeed established here by the lords of sages.
Thus ends the tenth chapter.
One should know that the *anudātta* (unaccented) tone is in the heart, the *udātta* (accented) is at the top of the head, and one should recognize the *svarita* (circumflex) at the root of the ear.

The accumulation [of tones] is traditionally taught to occur in every phonetic element (*pratīka*); this alone is the place for vowels, and nothing else. (72) The *svāra* is a combination; the acute (*udātta*) is high-pitched, while the grave (*anudātta*) is indeed low-pitched.
In continuous speech (*saṃhitā*), when following a circumflex (*svarita*), there may be one, two, or many grave vowels. (73)
Those which reside on a syllable and possess the quality consisting of the nature of the accumulated accent (pracaya-svara) here are called *uccaka-śruti*.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter.
When there is the substitution of *y* for an *i*-vowel at the beginning of a word, that which is accented (*svaryate*) in the case of two acute (*udātta*) vowels is the *kṣaipra* [svarita]. 74.

One should know that when a syllable preceded by *yava* is acutely accented (*svarita*) in a pause (*sthite pade*), even if it is preceded by a low-pitched (*nīca*) or unprecedented (*apūrvaka*) syllable, it is invariably *svarita*; here, the sequence [of preceding sounds] does not matter. Furthermore, even when situated in different words, that which is acutely accented according to the *saṃhitā* [rules] is called *prātihata*.

If, when [the preceding vowel] has been elided, there is a high-pitched (udātta) vowel standing in a separate word-position followed by a low-pitched (anudātta) vowel *a*, then this [resulting] svarita accent would be called "abhihata" (struck); furthermore, if a low-pitched quality (*anudāttadharmaka*) vowel *u* follows a high-pitched vowel *u* in a joined (saṃdhi) state, it becomes [svarita]. 76–77.

This [svarita] is indeed the combination of both [the udātta and anudātta], and it is called *praśliṣṭa* by the wise when it occurs within the same word (*samāne pade*). As for that *vivṛtti* which occurs in the same word, the svarita obtained after it is called *pādavṛtta* and nothing else; of this *vivṛtti* as well, the duration is half a mora (*ardhamātra*).
When the syllable is identical, that which is preceded by an udātta vowel is *tairovyañjana* when followed by a consonant.

(79) In the case of *kṣepa* and *nitya*, an extremely firm effort (*ati-dṛḍha-prayatna*) is required; in *abhihata*, a firm effort (*dṛḍha-prayatna*) preceded by "extremely" (*ati-pūrva*) is to be applied;
in *praśliṣṭaka* and *prātihata*, the same applies, while in *svarita*, an extremely soft effort (*ati-mṛdu-prayatna*) is likewise required. (80)
"In the *pādavṛtta* and indeed in the *sapṛkta*, when there is a *svarita* [vowel], the effort should be even less.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.
Where there are *praśliṣṭa*, *nityābhihata*, and *kṣaipra* [sandhis], as well as those followed by a high-pitched (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) vowel, [the effort is minimal]. 81.

In that regard, these [vowels] are indeed subject to *kampa* at the juncture (*sandhi*) following a preceding vowel; one should treat what is struck [by the pause] as having *kampa*. Just as a long vowel is pronounced, so too should a short vowel be pronounced with *kampa*.
(82) *Kampa* is of two kinds: *svarita* and *udātta*; however, here in the *saṃhitā*, those called *svarita-kampa* [are intended].
In other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*), there are indeed "tremblings of the acute" (*udāttakampa*); those two are further divided into short and long.
Of that [acute], at the beginning it has the natural tone (*svarita*) for a duration of three *aṇu*-measures; at its end, when struck, it is one *aṇu*-measure.
Likewise, the high [pitch] is three *aṇu*-measures at the beginning, and at its final part, it is low by one *aṇu*-measure.
In the conjunction of those two, that very [vowel] is a tremor (*kampa*) of two morae (*mātrā*); and in the case of *svarita* and *udātta*, there is a tremor of the *kṣaipra*.
However, for the *eṅ* sound struck by *ādūt* and *aidūt*, the tremor consists of four [morae].
Here, the *praśliṣṭa* is said to be constant due to the substitution of *ū*; it is called *āt* in some cases, and *oṅ* from *eṅ*.

Thus, *eṅ* and *ru* are eternal; the acute accent (*udātta*) and the kampita have been explained in this manner, and the determination of *kampa* is thus concluded. Chapter Thirteen, titled "The Determination of *Kampa*," ends here.
Furthermore, the term *svarabhakti* applies to a spirant (*ūṣman*) that follows a vowel, as well as to the *repha* and the letter *la* when they follow a vowel.

In the case of *ra* and *la*, there may be a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) at the beginning and end [of a consonant cluster], joined with a minute portion (*aṇumātrā*) of the vowel. Since *ra* and *la* are joined with a quarter-part of a vowel, they are therefore designated as "vowel-fragments" (*svarabhakti*).
That which ends in a consonant preceded by two quarters of the preceding part is called "contracted" (*saṃvṛta*); however, when followed by *ha*, it is simply a "fragment" (*bhakti*). (87–88)
When joined with another consonant, the *bhakti* [vowel] occurs before *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*; when followed by another vowel, it is called *vivṛtābhidhānā*.
Having abandoned the triad consisting of the shortness of the preceding vowel, *ikāra*, and *ukāra*, one should indeed utter the *bhakti*.
When combined with *ra* and *ha*, it is designated as *kareṇu*; when combined with *la* and *ha*, it becomes *karviṇī*.
When there is the letter *ra*, the *haṃsapada* occurs between a *yoga* (consonant cluster) and a vowel; when *śa* and *sa* are above it, it becomes the *hariṇī*.
Some call that vowel-fragment (*svarabhakti*) which occurs in the conjunction of *ra* and *sa* the "elephant" (*hastinī*).
However, the fragment that occurs here in the word *syadhūrṣam* is said to be an independent *svarabhakti*.
That [vowel] would be *hāritā* in the same manner for the *laśa* notes; thus, there are those divisions of the seven notes (*svarabhakti*) in sequence.
This is the fourteenth chapter.
I shall now illustrate those *svarabhaktis* in order, beginning with *kareṇu* and ending with *hāritā*. (92)

One who sacrifices the *barhis* is worthy of the *gārhapatya*; a female elephant (*kareṇu*) that is large might be a *karviṇī*; one with a bull (*saharṣabhā*) is a *haṃsapadā*. A *suvarṣa* is a *darśa* and a *parśu*, while a *hariṇī* is a *barsa*. 93. Regarding that *barsa*, later on it is said "either a female elephant" or "the yoke-pole of Truth" (*ṛtasya dhūrṣā*), and likewise "independent" (*svatantrā*).
"O Śatavalśa, they are indeed like the Harita tree with its thousand branches; thus have they been illustrated through the divisions of the seven notes.
(94) Thus ends the fifteenth chapter.
Furthermore, from a long vowel, a short vowel, or a svarita vowel that is not final, there arises a distinct *bhakti* which is uncombined (*asaṃhitā*).
When a syllable here possesses a distinct vowel sound and there is a separate division, the *nihata* does not occur above [the vowel].
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter.
In this context, the non-coalescence (*asandhi*) of two vowels is indeed called *vivṛtti* by those who know it.

The Krama-vatsānusṛti, the Vatsānusāriṇī, the Pākavatī, the Pipīlikā (96), the Vaiśeṣikā, the Ubhayadīrghikā, the Madhyamā, and the Savarṇatā—these are indeed the eight varieties known as Vivṛtti; their true nature shall now be described here. (97)

If there is a long vowel preceded by a short one and followed by a long one, that is indeed a *vatsānusṛti* consisting of two morae (*mātrā*). However, where a long vowel is preceded by a short one, even if it follows the pattern of a *vatsānusāriṇī*, it consists of only one mora.
In a *vivṛtti* where there is a short vowel on both sides, it is indeed three-quarters of a mora (*pādona-mātrā*) according to the *Pākavatī* school.
Successively, the long vowels in the preceding and following [syllables] are high and low respectively at the time of the word; 99.

And where a *visarjanīya* is not seen, and where a *svarita* is obtained through *saṃdhi*, even though they have become homogeneous (*savarṇa*), those two should be considered as having the measure of a quarter (*pādamātrā*) and being like an ant (*pipīlikā*). 100.

There may be a modification (*vivṛtti*) where, at the beginning and end [of a word], there is a long vowel resulting from the combination of non-homogeneous vowels (*asavarṇa-dīrgha*), and in the middle there may or may not be a *visarga*; this is the specific rule regarding the duration of one mora (*mātrikakāla*).

Furthermore, when there is a long vowel resulting from the combination of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-dīrgha*) at the beginning and end, there is no *visarga* in the word resulting from the euphonic junction (*sandhāna-pada*).
That [vowel] in which such qualities exist, and which possesses one mora that is long in both places, is [the *madhyamā*].

(102) If there exists [a vowel] where there is a homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*) on both sides, and where the acute (*udātta*) and grave (*nīca*) accents occur in sequence, and if there is a *visarjanīya* therein, it is also a *svāra*; and in the case of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*), it is a *madhyamā* consisting of one mora. (103)

At the beginning and likewise at the end, there is the long vowel by class-similarity (*savarṇadīrgha*); when [the compound] is analyzed, it is accompanied by a *visarjanīya*, and in that case, there is never a circumflex (*svarita*) accent. Its duration is one *mātrā*, for the long vowel by class-similarity consists of one *mātrā*. Alternatively, if there is an *anunāsika* (nasalized) sound in the middle of the *vāk* (speech-unit), then that *anunāsika* has a duration of one and a quarter *mātrās*.
That manifestation (*vyakti*) here also consists of one and a quarter *mātrās*, and its name is the same as that previously mentioned.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter.
Now he will illustrate the *vivṛtti*s, beginning with *vatsānusṛti* and ending with *savarṇatā*.
They bring us further life; he follows after his offspring. 106.
Whether it be that which follows the calf or this [earth] which was here in the beginning, he is born with the people.
For Indra, the deliverer from distress, [I offer] the *pra-uga* hymn, the *pākavatī*, and Indra himself. 107.
Or, if an ant were to come upon him while he was being carried away from the beginning, those very ants would be such; likewise, Kakṣīvat Auśija would be those designated by the Vaiśeṣika school.
Or, if water were to flow for him in that same way, it would be a double-long channel. 108–109.

Or rather, those which are the Āgrayaṇa and the foremost of the offerings, and those which are the Āpri verses in the middle, and those which are the Āpri verses for the gods— these waters they call the "long-vowel of identical color" (svarṇadīrghī).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter.
Yaśas, Mamā, Sumaṅgalā, Ślokopahūtā, and likewise Yadghrāt—these indeed are the five *raṅgas*. Of them, I shall now describe the characteristics of their sequence of syllables (*varṇakrama*).
In the *raṅga* called *mukha*, there should be two morae (*mātrā*) resembling the roar of a tiger, produced in the heart but not from the mouth.
Now, here, a single-mora sound like the resonance of a bronze bell, accompanied by a tremor, arising from the head;
at the end, one that flows out through both nostril-pores and is a single mora—that would be the *kākalī*.
It is like the cry "takrā" uttered with a beautiful throat-voice by a cowherd’s wife from Saurāṣṭra. 112–113.
Having thus pronounced [the mantra], one should speak from its own time; indeed, that *raṅga* and *kampa* increase.
This is the nineteenth chapter.
O gods, these [syllables] are indeed immortal; I shall place them in my throat; truly, they are long and moving (*raṅgadīrghāḥ*). 114.

These [vowels] consist of two mātrās each, joined with a nasal sound of one and a quarter mātrās; following the *vivṛtti* (opening), there is one [mātrā] in the three sets of one and a quarter mātrās in the heart, and then half a mātrā in the head.
There is a distinction in the mouth and nose, and for that manifestation as well, it is of the size of an atom (*aṇumātra*).
Thus ends the twentieth chapter.
A consonant preceded by a vowel [becomes double] when followed by a *hal* (consonant); a stop (*sparśa*) preceded by the letter *la* becomes two syllables.
Furthermore, when a *hal* follows a *repha* (the sound *r*) preceded by a vowel, doubling occurs before any subsequent phoneme.

A *ṅ* at the end of a word becomes two-colored (nasalized) when followed by a vowel, as does a *ṇ* preceded by a short vowel even if it occurs in the middle of a word. In the *Yajurveda*, where there is an *anusvāra*, it likewise becomes two-colored when joined with the first half of a *ga* sound, provided that the following letter is *śa*; however, this does not apply to a *ga* that is designated as "simple" (*kevala*). 117–118.

After a short vowel, *anusvāra* [is inserted] before a consonant cluster (*iy-ādi*) consisting of two phonemes when followed by another [consonant]; and that [cluster] shall consist of one mora (*mātrika*).
Here, the beginning of the cluster is likewise doubled, even if preceded by *anusvāra*; furthermore, there may be an augment (*āgama*). 119.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter.

Whatever consonant, by whatever cause, attains a double color at this very moment, there shall indeed be a prior arrival (doubling) here for the second and fourth [consonants] respectively. This is the path of the supreme prefixes (upasarga) when they have become exceedingly powerful; these [prefixes], beginning with *ati*, are those that have gone upward (*atyūrdhvagata*). They are the possessors of the hands (*bhujāḥ*) which are the letters *cha* and *kha*.

These three [consonants] would indeed attain that first and third preceding augment (pūrvāgama) as their locus. However, in certain cases where there is a similarity between two vowels, a pair of consonants may occur according to the observed usage (lakṣya); for in such instances, the preceding augment would belong to the second or the fourth [consonant] of the word, precisely according to the observed usage.
In the Taittirīya, there is indeed the substitution of *ña* for *ś*; however, this does not occur in the Kāṭhaka.
When a sibilant (*ūṣman*) followed by a stop (*sparśa*) is preceded by another [stop], there is here an augment (*āgama*) consisting of the position of that [preceding] stop.
Furthermore, the first letter of the class (*varga-prathama*) occurs once, and it is here called *abhinidhāna*. In this context, *abhinidhāna* is so designated.
When a nasal (ṅ) follows, then two augmentations, *k* and *g*, both occur after an anusvāra. 124.
When a non-final (anuttama) stop (*sparśa*) or a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows without modification, a final (uttama) [stop] occurs above it according to the regular sequence;
these are called "nasals" (*nāsikya*) here, and they are considered augmentations (*āgama*). Some call these very ones "the *yamas*. 125.

The first [consonant], reaching the end of the word, pervades and takes on the second letter situated at the end of the word, provided that the following two [letters] are not situated at the end of a word; such is the case in *paśau* (Paśupati). In this sequence of letters, the sound following a short vowel is of two forms; the knower should utter it only once.

When duality is set aside because it has already occurred, that is called "prior arrival" (pūrvāgama) here. [Verse 127] The sounds *ī*, *ai*, *ay*, and so forth; the visarga and the *repha* (*r*); the sibilants (*ūṣman*) before a vowel or a stop (*sparśa*) followed by a first or second [surd] mute; and the letter *v*—these, when standing after a sibilant or a stop, may take two forms. [Verse 128]

When followed by another letter of the same class (*savarṇa*) that is not final, a consonant undergoes doubling; however, this should be understood to apply only when the following [consonant] is a stop (*sparśa*). If it is followed by *y*, *v*, or *l*, then *m* [is doubled] as well, and for those [stops], the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form is also used. (129) Furthermore, after a long vowel, the *n* at the end of a word is optionally doubled, and the same applies to *y* and *h*.
Where a visarga is seen before the letters śa, ṣa, or sa, that is the state of modification (vaikṛtatva);
whereas where ṇa, ṇa, ma, or ya are seen following the letter ha, that is the state of the original (prākṛtatva), occurring respectively in a case of phonetic fusion (śliṣṭa). 130–131.
In that context, the nasality and the chest-origin (of the *ha*) are mentioned twice;
where there is a visarga between two open vowels (*vivṛtta*), it consists of half a mora (*ardhamātrika*). A pause (*virāma*) shall consist of one mora; its designation is according to the rule.
If a visarga occurs before the vowels *i* and *u*, or before the consonants *k* and *p* respectively, it is called the jihvāmūlīya and the upadhmānīya;
it is said to be the name for that which expresses a sound devoid of a vowel. 133–134.
"In the study of the sequence of phonemes, one should not utter that which bears another name"—thus ends the twenty-second chapter.
However, when a pure phoneme occurs at the beginning of a word, if *uc* and so forth are employed [as substitutes], [the rule applies]. 135.
One should discern its own vowel and consonant; this indeed is its defining characteristic.

Regarding the consonant, the vowel, the measure (mātrā), the limbs (aṅga), and the essence of the consonants, there is never a conjunction (saṃdhi) occurring before the vowels following the letter *ka*. 136.

If the Mātṛkā is joined with a vowel before an accented (udātta) or other vowel-sound, that Mātṛkā is called a "vowel" (varṇa) within the name; however, if it is joined with a vowel (ac) before that [consonant], it is designated as a "vowel" (saṃjñā) prior to the Mātṛkā. 137–138.
"Let there be the designation 'aṅga' for the *hal* [consonants] at the beginning; its names are the 'descriptions of the limbs' (*aṅgavarṇaka*).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, wherein, according to the prescription of the sequence of consonants, [the rules are established]. 139.

Just as the characteristics of the limbs have been declared, one should speak likewise regarding the color of the limbs; however, regarding the consonants in the color of the limbs, one should state the limb as having one more than the number of elements (bhūta).
Then, by the explicit statement "known as *ha*," one should indeed utter that name.
First, one should state the designation "vowel" (ac) for the vowels, followed by their respective measures (mātrā).
Then, one should state the vowels—whether udātta and so forth—and their names in sequence.
If a consonant follows, its measure is prescribed [as half]. 141–142.
Where that [consonant] remains uncombined, its corresponding *mātrā* is not accepted there;

where there is a conjunction of multiple vowels consisting of a single consonant, it shall be the preceding limb (*pūrvāṅga*), and in that case, one should pronounce the preceding limb and so forth only once. 143.

If a combination of two consonants were to involve both members [of the pair] as a single unit, then one should apply them as separate members according to their sequential order; in that case, the doubling and so forth of a single phoneme that was taught by the treatise would apply. 144–145.
One should employ all of that in the description of the qualities of the limbs according to the rule.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter;
the *Pāriśikṣā* is completed.
